utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours now having had the opportunity to read the skeleton argument we have presented, Your Honours, may I just take you briefly through what we submit are the correct and relevant principles that Your Honours should apply when dealing with the admission of documentary evidence? Your Honours, we have to start with the rule obviously. I notice it's absent from Mr. Ackerman's skeleton argument. However Rule 89 starts by saying, in terms, "A Chamber shall apply the rules of evidence set forth in this Section, and shall not be bound by national rules of evidence." And then it deals, after setting out the principle, with the basis of admission. In Rule 89(C), "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." (D), "A Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." And then (E), "A Chamber may request verification of the authenticity of evidence obtained out of court." Your Honour, therefore our first submission is this: That Rule 89 establishes a presumption in favour of admission and places the burden on the objecting party to articulate how the principles of fairness demand that the evidence should be excluded under Subrule (D). Your Honours, if I may digress just very briefly, we would submit this: That the clear philosophy and the guiding principle of the Tribunal's approach to the admission of evidence is an inclusive one, without the regard for technical or procedural rules which are the characteristic of some national systems, as Mr. Ackerman refers to those -- he says the United Kingdom. I happen to know the Scots take a very dim view of that. It's the principles in England and Wales, the Scottish approach is very different. But one of the reasons, of course, for these highly technical rules is because there and in the United States, it operates largely on a jury system. Here, of course, as the Tribunal has so often stated, one is dealing with professional Judges. Your Honours, the manner in which the admissibility of evidence has been treated, and the principles, are very similar also to those that were dealt with in the Nuremberg trials. One has to remember that the documents here, as they were in Nuremberg, were gathered as a result of search warrants, of submission by interested parties, and Your Honour is going to hear evidence about that shortly. But really, what one is talking about is a situation of gathering material from a country that is largely hostile - or great parts of it - to the aims -- or was hostile to the aims of this Tribunal. And in Nuremberg, one of the things that was clearly stated was this, that - this was in Article 7 of Ordinance number 7, and it's very similar to this Tribunal's rule. "The Tribunals shall not be bound by technical rules of evidence. They shall adopt and apply to the greatest possible extent expeditious and non-technical procedure and shall admit any evidence which they deem to have probative value." Now, Your Honour, if one moves on to the cases where these matters have arisen, really one starts with the case of Delalic which was decided on the 19th of January, 1998, in which Mr. Ackerman appeared, as Your Honours have seen. This was -- the basis of the application was to exclude the -- the Defence applied to exclude documents that had been obtained by a search conducted by the Austrian police in 1996, and in delivering their judgement, having dealt with the arguments that had been raised, can I draw Your Honours' attention, please, to the rulings which begin at page 7, paragraph 15, "Findings," where the principles are set out in paragraph 15? The question before the Trial Chamber is that of the admissibility of evidence: A matter where the national legal systems of the world have adopted diverging approaches, the procedure of the International Tribunal, with its unique mixture of common and civil law features, does not conform to any one tradition in this respect. In contrast to the common law, where questions of admissibility and exclusion of evidence occupy a prominent place in criminal procedure, the ten provisions of the Rules which regulate all evidentiary matters in the proceedings before the International Tribunal do not contain a detailed set of technical rules relating to this issue. The question of admissibility of evidence before the International Tribunal is governed by Section 3 of the Rules, which is entitled "Rules of Evidence." The approach adopted by the Rules is clearly one in favour of admissibility, as long as the evidence is relevant and is deemed to have probative value, Subrule 89(C), and its probative value is not substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial, Subrule 89(D). And then it deals with the other applications -- the other Rules. Of these provisions, Subrule 89(C) is of particular pertinence to the issue before the Trial Chamber. According to the plain text of this provision, the two requirements for the admissibility of evidence are those of relevance and probative value. And then it goes on to say: "In relation of the question of the substantive meaning of these requirements, the Trial Chamber notes that evidence which is of probative value within the common law tradition has been defined as evidence that tends to prove an issue. As concerns relevance, it is often said that this concept in itself contains an implicit requirement of probative value." And it then deals with authorities, which at that stage - because this was in the early stages of the Tribunal - were drawn from other jurisdictions. It then in paragraph 19 - I can move to that - effectively raise doubt with the argument which is now being raised before Your Honours. "The Defence contends, however, that a determination of reliability should be seen as a separate first step in assessing a piece of evidence offered for admission and argues that it is only if this first hurdle has been passed that the Trial Chamber can proceed to consider the relevance and probative value of the evidence." And again, this is very much the issue that is raised by Mr. Ackerman in his submissions to Your Honour. This view of reliability as a separate requirement, independent of those provided for my Subrule 89(C) has been rejected by the Trial Chamber in the Mucic handwriting decision. As the Trial Chamber there noted, it is a cardinal rule of construction of legislation that where the words of a provision are clear and unambiguous, the task of interpretation does not arise. So it is with Subrule 89(C), and it is therefore neither necessary nor desirable to add to that provision a condition of admissibility which is not expressly prescribed for by that provision. "Whilst the importance of the Rules on admissibility in common law follows from the effect which the admission of a certain piece of evidence might have on a group of lay jurors, the trials before the International Tribunal are conducted by professional Judges who by virtue of their training and experience are able to consider each piece of evidence which has been admitted and determine its appropriate weight. As noted above, it is an implicit requirement of the Rules that the Trial Chamber give due considerations to indicia of reliability when assessing the relevance and probative value of evidence at the stage of determining its admissibility. However, this terminology may leave some room for misunderstanding and could possibly be misperceived as demanding that a binding determination be made at this stage as to the genuineness, authorship, or credibility of evidence. For this reason, the Trial Chamber wishes to make it clear that the mere admission of a document into evidence does not in and of itself signify that the statements contained therein will necessarily be deemed to be an accurate portrayal of the facts. Factors such as authenticity and proof of authorship will naturally assume the greatest importance in the Trial Chamber's assessment of the weight to be attached to individual pieces of evidence. The threshold standard for the admission of evidence, however, should not be set excessively high, as often documents are sought to be admitted into evidence not as ultimate proof of guilt or innocence but to provide a context and complete the picture presented by the evidence gathered."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Paragraph 22: "It is clear from the relevant provision of the Rules that there is no blanket prohibition on the admission of documents simply on the ground that the purported author has not been called to testify in the proceedings. Instead, the conditions for admissibility are those contained in Subrule 89(C), which have been discussed above." And Your Honour, I don't think I need go any further because they dealt then with the documents. Your Honour, that decision was upheld by the Appeals Chamber. Your Honours will find that decision behind - behind - divider 3. And they simply upheld the decision that had been made. Though if I can draw Your Honour's attention to paragraph 20, which is at page 9: "It is to be noted that the Trial Chamber in this case stated that a decision to admit a piece of evidence does not influence in any way the weight it would later attach to that evidence. The applicant appears to have confused a question relating to admissibility with that as to weight. The implicit requirement that a piece of evidence be prima facie credible, that it have sufficient indicia of reliability, is a factor in assessment of its relevance and probative value. To require absolute proof of a document's authenticity before it could be admitted would be to require a far more stringent test than the standard envisioned by Subrule 89." Your Honour, allowing for the interpreters, perhaps we could just have a quick canter, if that's the right word, or a slow trot through the other authorities, all of which we submit are to the same effect. In the Prosecutor against Blaskic, in which Mr. Cayley appeared, there was a decision on the 30th of January, 1998, which is the second one copied. And the Trial Chamber there decided, if I can take Your Honours to the decision at page 10: "Any documentary evidence produced by a party and identified by a witness shall be admitted. Should a challenge to the authenticity of such a document arise, the document will be admitted but that the weight to be ascribed to it will depend on the additional elements which will have, if necessary, been provided and which permit attesting to its authenticity." Your Honour, if I may digress for a moment into this case, we are asking Your Honours to admit evidence on the basis that we can show from where that evidence has been obtained, and as the case goes on, it is anticipated that witnesses will come and be able to add to the authenticity of that document because they will have seen it in some form or another. This is particularly true, for example, of the Variant A and B document, about which Your Honours were not obliged to hear evidence because the objection to authenticity was withdrawn, but Your Honours would have heard how it had been referred to in speeches, how it had been published in a newspaper and the like. Your Honours, then dealing with the remaining authorities, which we have provided copies of, the next case in time was the Kvocka case, the Omarska case. The order of the 17th of March, 1999, where the only really additional matter that I should draw your attention to in page 2 of the very short decision, that the -- it was ordered that the documents listed in annex 1 of the request -- I may say there were very many items in that annex -- "that the Defence are at liberty to challenge the authenticity of any of the documents during the trial and the Prosecution shall deal with any issues raised as to the authenticity of the documents so admitted by way of rebuttal." Your Honour, the next case that we have referred to, again involved the case against Blaskic. One can see how long it went on, on the basis the first decision was in 1998 and this one was in March of 2000. We've only copied part of the judgement because other parts dealt with other matters and this was the only part that dealt with admissibility. In paragraph 34: "The admissibility of the evidence presented at trial was also the subject of decisions on several occasions. The principle embodied by the case law of the Trial Chamber on the issue is the one of extensive admissibility of evidence, questions of credibility or authenticity being determined according to the weight given to each of the materials by the Judges at the appropriate time." And Your Honours, finally, we have copied for Your Honours the three decisions in the case of Sikirica, which was the Keraterm camp case. Your Honour, effectively, it just repeats what was said in the earlier decisions relating to the case of Kvocka. Your Honours, in summary, therefore, we make the submissions that we've set out in the skeleton argument to Your Honours. We submit that for a document to be admitted into evidence, the Prosecution must establish relevance and probative value, but it need not establish authenticity or authorship or even the source, according to some of the decisions, of the document for such admission. We will, however, for Your Honours, if required, establish - and for my learned friends - establish the source. Your Honour, we submit that the submissions made orally last Friday and in writing by Mr. Ackerman are misguided, because they refer -- the whole of Mr. Ackerman's submission is based upon national rules, and we submit that the rules which apply in national jurisdictions - for example, as we heard in the former Yugoslavia, documents had to have a date or a seal or a signature, or the stringent rules referred to in England and Wales or in the United States, or in Your Honour's own jurisdiction - may be of assistance when there has been no jurisprudence from the Tribunal on the matter, and they are sometimes persuasive or help Judges decide something which has not been decided before, but we submit are of no relevance where there is clear and unambiguous authority on the point and in this case, coming from the Appeals Chamber, not just other Trial Chambers. So we submit finally that unless the Defence raise the issue - we do not suggest the burden lies upon them, but it is for them to at least raise a credible issue that a document or a set of documents are irrelevant or have no probative value, or that their probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial - then we submit, other than that happening, the document should be admitted into evidence. Your Honours, those are the submissions we make on behalf of the Prosecution in this matter. Your Honours, may I add that if Your Honours think that the skeleton argument was of any assistance, I should say that it was largely prepared - because I don't think that enough credit is given - to an intern working here who did this over the weekend, and I think he deserves credit for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Fauveau, is it all right if I start with Mr. Ackerman or would you like to start yourself?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may start with Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and thank you. It's quite clear, I think, at this point that the Prosecutor has a fundamental and basic misunderstanding of the issue and the objections that are being made with regard to documents in this case. And given a few moments here, I think I can probably clarify that and the Chamber -- give the Chamber some indication of exactly where it is that we are trying to suggest that matters need to be treated properly. I want to first comment very briefly on Ms. Korner's initial suggestion to you that things should be treated differently here in the Tribunal because of the nature of the way the documents are gathered, that they are gathered by search warrants, usually from persons who are hostile to the Prosecution's position. In 30 years of trying cases, both as counsel and as a judge in the United States, most of the documents that come into criminal trials in the United States are gathered by search warrant from persons who are hostile to the position of the Prosecution. So there is not a large difference there. The second thing, just as a preliminary matter, that I want to point out is that the rules of evidence that exist both in England, Wales, and in the United States that I have referred to do not have exceptions. The rules of evidence in the United States do not have exceptions for cases that are not being tried to a jury. The rules apply with the same force in trials before a judge as they do to a trial by jury. I want to begin, rather than with my memorandum, with the material that was provided to you by Ms. Korner, because those cases are in complete agreement, absolutely complete agreement, with what we are arguing to you and have been arguing to you since the beginning of this case. Since I was in the Delalic case, I can tell you some of the background of how this issue came before the Court in Delalic. The Prosecution had a number of documents. When I say a number of documents, one must not confuse it in any way with the number of documents we have in this case. It was a fairly limited number of documents. I think they could all be put into two binders, as I recall. I could be wrong about that. I think it's two binders of documents or less. These documents were seized by search warrant by the Austrian police from a business office in Vienna that was a place where one of the defendants in the case, Mr. Delalic, worked and kept records and documents. So we start with the proposition that they came from a place where there was some indication that they belonged to and were kept there by one of the defendants in the case. That in itself is indicia of reliability of the documents. We then had days of testimony - when I say "days," I think we may have gone for a week - with Officer Moerbauer from the Vienna police, who described in great detail the process by which these documents were seized, the law under which they were seized, the regularity of the process by which they were seized, and the way that they were marked by the Austrian police and delivered to the Tribunal. So there was significant evidence about the source of these documents, how they came into the possession of the Prosecutor, and that the documents we had in court were in fact the same documents that came from Moerbauer in Vienna. As I say, that went on for days. We had in the case, representing Mr. Mucic a gentleman by the name of Mr. Greaves from Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and Mr. Greaves was arguing for what I have set out in my memorandum to you as the English position regarding authenticity. He was arguing that the Trial Chamber should adopt the English standard in this Court which would require the Prosecutor to prove authenticity beyond a reasonable doubt. That, the Trial Chamber did not agree with. And Ms. Korner read to you a section of the decision where they said they would not require absolute proof of authenticity, and that's what the Chamber was referring to. It was the Greaves argument that the proof should be beyond a reasonable doubt. Now, if you go to -- there were two basic decisions that came out of the Celebici Trial Chamber. One of them had to do with these documents from Vienna. Another had to do with -- I believe it was some issue regarding a statement or something with Mucic, but in any event what the Chamber said, that reliability is necessary to be established, sufficient indicia of reliability needs to be established as a condition to the admissibility under Rule 89(C), not that it requires absolute proof but there must be sufficient indicia of reliability with regard to the document. And that's what I suggest to you in the memorandum that I gave you this morning. Rather than arguing for the very strict British rule, I suggest that what would be appropriate before this Tribunal, and what seems to be already the law of this Tribunal, and that is simply a prima facie case put forward that the document is reliable before it becomes part of evidence. Once it is shown to be reliable, then it is -- prima facie shown to be reliable, then it could be admitted, I would suggest, unless it's clear, at first blush, that it has no relevance or probative value to the case. In other words, if the Prosecutor were to come in here for an article from the New York Times regarding events in Panama that could not possibly be related to this case, even though there was a showing that it was reliable, the Court could say, "Wait a minute. This has no relevance. There is no sense letting it come in, even at this point." In page -- looking at the Celebici decision of 19 January, 1998, paragraph 20, with regard to this issue of authenticity: "Factors such as authenticity and proof of authorship will naturally assume the greatest importance in the Trial Chamber's assessment of the weight to be attached to individual pieces of evidence. The threshold standard for the admission of evidence should not be set excessively high, as often documents are sought to be admitted into evidence not as ultimate proof of guilt or innocence but to provide a context and complete the picture" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please. The interpreters do not have these texts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, she just told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What the Chamber is saying there, Your Honours, is that if the document is being offered in the trial only as -- not as ultimate proof of guilt or innocence, but only to provide a context and complete a picture presented by other evidence gathered, then one need not be quite so strict about the evidence regarding its reliability. But just before that, the Chamber is very clear: "Factors such as authenticity and proof of authorship will assume the greatest importance in the Trial Chamber's assessment of the weight to be attached to individual pieces of evidence." It's important. Now, this is a Trial Chamber decision. You have the option to follow that decision or not. The Blaskic decision of 30 January 1998 -- and I read it as rapidly as I could, but it appears to me that this decision is not on point at all in this sense: What was going on there was the Prosecutor had provided the Defence with some Rule 68 exculpatory documents, and the Defence was contending that the Prosecution had an obligation to also provide them with the evidence necessary to allow them to authenticate the documents, otherwise they would be deprived of the ability to use the exculpatory evidence in court. And the Prosecution was resisting that proposition and resisting the request that they provide that additional information. So it's really not the same thing. If one goes, then, to the Delalic appeal decision, which is binding upon this Chamber, again it's very clear that what we are suggesting is exactly what that case requires. "The implicit requirement of reliability" -- and for reliability, you can also read authenticity, and this is in paragraph 17: "The implicit requirement of reliability means no more than there must be sufficient indicia of reliability to make out a prima facie case," which is exactly what I am suggesting to you in my memorandum. That's what it requires, sufficient indicia of reliability to make out a prima facie case that the document is what the Prosecutor says it is. There is no way, Your Honours, that a document can be relevant or have probative value unless it is what the Prosecutor says it is. If the Prosecutor says, "I want to offer you a document that was authored by Radoslav Brdjanin," and it is not a document authored by Radoslav Brdjanin, it can't ever have any relevance or probative value. It cannot. And until there is some showing, a prima facie showing, that it is in fact what the Prosecutor says it is, you can't consider issues of weight or relevance or probative value because you don't know what the document is. Now, frequently, you can look at the document on its face, you can make a determination as to its reliability, because it has a stamp and it has a signature, and it is a regular document, it's the original, it comes from the place where that original should be. And sure enough, when you look there, there it is. And it requires nothing more then. It self-authenticates. And I understand it's the law of Yugoslavia that a document that has a stamp and a signature self-authenticates; it doesn't require any original proof of authenticity. But if that document that has no stamp and no signature and just the typewritten name of an individual on it, then something has to happen beyond just offering it to you. The Prosecution has to give you a prima facie showing that it is what they say it is. That's what was held by the Appeals Chamber in Celebici, that there must be a sufficient indicia of reliability to make out a prima facie case. Now, you go to these other orders, following after the Celebici appeal decision. Many of these orders you will see -- they are all pre-trial. None of them are orders that were entered during the trial of a case. Many of them involve situations where the Defence did not object to any of the documents at all, and so they were just admitted without Defence objection. These are all cases where the world of documents that was being considered is a small number. If we had five or six binders of documents in this case, or ten in this case, then it could make sense that we simply put them up here and begin to work with them as if they're evidence in the case, and it's real easy then to sort out the issues of whether they are reliable, whether the Court should consider them, because there are so few. We are engaging here in a whole new era of this Tribunal's life. This is the first case and will be followed by many more. I think of Plavsic and Krajisnik and Milosevic and some of the others to come that have this huge document base that the Tribunal has to figure out some way to deal with. And what we cannot do in a case of that magnitude is what is easier to do in some of the smaller cases. These cases involve maybe one municipality or some prison guards, as to whom there are virtually no documents. Rarely do you find a bunch of documents regarding prison guards. We're talking about leader -- alleged leadership people over a large area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we're talking about - I don't know, I haven't even counted - I think a thousand or more exhibits that are going to be offered to you in this case. We cannot adopt a way of handling them that would allow them to come into evidence, allow witnesses to testify as to their contents, on the proposition that somewhere, as Ms. Korner says, in the case a witness will come along that will provide some evidence of authenticity of that document. We will completely lose track of what we're doing and get completely off track, so that when we get to the end of the case, when we try to prepare our submissions to you about what is evidence in the case and what isn't, when you try to struggle with those documents and their relevance and their probative value and their weight, you will find that you are facing an almost impossible task. What has to happen is we have to limit this universe of documents in this case to those as to which there can be a prima facie case of reliability put by the Prosecutor. I set out in my memorandum to you what I think is -- are some of the ways. And I don't try to -- and I don't propose that these are all of the ways that a document can be authenticated in a prima facie way, but these are just examples of how I think it works. A witness with knowledge can say, "Yes, that document is what Ms. Korner says it is. I know. I was there. I saw it at the time it was issued." To some extent, that's a little bit of what we had with regard to the A/B. We had people signing other documents acknowledging the receipt of that particular document or referring to it. Identification -- number 2: "Identification of handwriting or the signature by a witness personally familiar with it or by expert comparison with known exemplar." So if you have a document that merely has a signature with no stamp and there's some contest regarding the genuineness of that document or the signature, then provide a witness. Chances are that will happen rarely, very rarely, because what's happening right now with regard to these documents is both parties are waiving foundation, waiving the establishment of reliability with regard to documents that have stamps and signatures on them. There's no sense challenging those. They are prima facie reliable. 3: "Distinctive characteristics such as paper, print, identifying marks, letterhead, seals, stamps which would ordinarily be associated with the claim source of the document, or being found in a place" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm doing it. -- "found in a place where documents of that kind would ordinarily be kept." And the fourth way that I suggest indicia of reliability can be shown is by "reference to its content, where it contains facts which would be known solely or particularly to the purported author or where it is consistent with established events relating to it." So for instance, if a witness comes here and says that on such and such a day troops entered a particular city and were there for three days, and then a document is presented later on which says on a certain day troops entered that city and were there for three days, even though it has no signature, it has indicia of reliability because it agrees with testimony that we've already heard. And that's the -- a kind of document that can be admitted without any further proof. But there has to be proof with regard to some of these documents. There just has to be. And when you see the documents, when you begin to look at them, you'll begin to understand that what you have before you is a giant pile of documents that came from a number of different places. You need to know where they came from to make any kind of a judgement about them. And many of them have nothing on their face to suggest that they have any reliability whatsoever. There are documents that are just typewritten and in capitals at the bottom, there is a name like "Milos," and there are many, many, many of those. And until you know that there is some way that those can be seen as reliable, then you can't give them any kind of weight, you can't find them to be relevant, you can't find them to be probative. A precondition to questions of relevance is that the document is what the proponent says it is. If it's not what the proponent says it is, then it can't possibly be said to be relevant or probative or given any weight. And that's all we're suggesting. And I'm not suggesting the English heavy burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt, just a prima facie case. And I think it's necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to be very brief, Mr. President, Your Honours, because my colleague Mr. Ackerman has presented his own conclusions, and I would like to associate myself to everything he has said. I only have one or two things to add. First, it is true that Rule 89 of the Rules of Procedure requires for a document to be admissible that it should be relative and have probative value. Nevertheless, it seems to me that a document that is not credible can certainly not have probative value and cannot be relevant. Also, in the decision which the Prosecutor gave us today, the Celebici judgement, the Chamber said that if the evidence is not credible, it cannot be -- it cannot have probative value. Consequently, evidence which is not credible and which is not relevant and does not have probative value is inadmissible. Something else I would like to add refers to Yugoslav documents with no signature or stamps. We are not contesting because according to Yugoslav law they are inadmissible. We contest them because according to Yugoslav national law, only a document that has a stamp and a signature is an authentic document, and vice versa. All documents that do not have a stamp or signature, there is a doubt, a suspicion, that this document may not be authentic, and that is the only reason why we are contesting those documents, because prima facie those documents are not authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I have a -- we have a right of reply, but I -- just two matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even if you didn't, I would grant it to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER

But in any event, we have to submit this to Your Honours, that in many cases, we're not dealing with official documents. Your Honour, we say that the test is relevance, probative value, and for these purposes we can establish the source for all the documents that we wish to put before Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. And after you, Ms. Fauveau, and that will be the end, and we'll break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Very brief. I didn't argue to you that weight must be established before admissibility, as Ms. Korner just said. And you know that I didn't argue that. And that's all I have to say.

utterances.text: Would you like to add or rebut something?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecutor had told us that we are not working here with official documents. But the documents that we are contesting do come from the municipal authorities or other official organs, so these would be official documents. They are the documents that bear no stamp or signature and that we are contesting. Secondly, if we don't know the source of a document, how can we know that that document is authentic, that it is not false?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That brings the debate on this issue to an end, at least for the time being. We will now go in Chambers. As I already explained to you, this is a subject that we had time to think about and research over the weekend, like you did. So more or less we are already very much prepared to come forward with an oral decision. As I explained to you, later on there will be -- the oral decision will be incorporated in a written one, which would, for record purposes in particular, incorporate also the various submissions that you have made. Now, you will realise that the various submissions that you have made will result from the transcript of this sitting. It doesn't mean to say that you are excluded from filing in the records of the case the submissions that you -- the memoranda that you have furnished the Chamber with this morning. You are at liberty to do that or not to do that. I mean, there is absolutely no requirement that you do. But irrespective of whether you do that or not, the submissions that you have made will be incorporated in the written decision which will be forthcoming in the next few days. In the meantime, I suppose that if we break for -- if we break for one hour, it should give us enough time to go through what we have already prepared, plus/minus, and come back at quarter to noon, quarter to 12.00, and give an oral decision. utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry for the delay but we needed an extra 30 minutes. So here we are and the Trial Chamber will proceed with its oral decision. In the course of last Friday's sitting, following some disagreement between the Prosecution and the Defence on various basic issues related to the admission of several documents in evidence, and with a view to delineating and setting down the rules which would be applied by this Trial Chamber in admitting or excluding evidence, particularly documentary evidence, learned counsel for the Prosecution asked for this issue to be debated during today's sitting, following which this Trial Chamber was then prayed to pronounce itself orally. As you know, the relative debate took place earlier on this morning and now that the Trial Chamber has been seized with this important issue and having considered the oral submissions of the parties, decides as follows: 1: In matters of admissibility of evidence, the procedure of this International Tribunal, with its unique mixture of common and civil law rules on procedure and evidence, rather than purporting to conform to any particular system or tradition, is inspired by the need for a fair determination of the matter before it. 2: The question of admissibility of evidence before this International Tribunal is governed by Section 3 of the Rules, entitled "Rules of Evidence." As explained in the Delalic Trial Chamber decision referred to in the course of this morning's oral submissions, the approach adopted by the Rules is clearly one in favour of admissibility, as long as the evidence is relevant and is deemed to have probative value, this in terms of Subrule 89(C), and also, as long as its probative value is not substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. Evidence may further be excluded on the grounds given in Rules 95 and 96. Subrule 89(E) relates to the authentication of evidence out of Court. Finally, Subrule 89(B), perhaps one of the most important rules of evidence, contains a provision of a residual nature which, in cases not otherwise provided for in the Rules, permits the application of such rules of evidence as will best favour a fair determination of the matter in question and which are consistent with the Statute and general principles of law. 3: As already stated by the Trial Chamber in Prosecutor versus Delalic, the same judgement that I referred to earlier and which was referred to earlier on this morning by both parties, "In contrast to the common law, where questions of admissibility and exclusion of evidence occupy a prominent place in criminal procedure, the ten" - now actually there are more - "provisions of the Rules which regulate all evidentiary matters in the proceedings before the International Tribunal do not contain a detailed set of technical rules relating to this issue." 4: It is therefore clear to this Trial Chamber that in the context of Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the approach of the Statute of this International Tribunal is to lay down a framework or a structure conceived in the broadest terms, providing that in the determination of the charges against him or her, the accused shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing. The Trial Chamber is in duty bound and therefore has the responsibility to ensure that the trial is fair and expeditious and that the proceedings are conducted in accordance with the Rules, with full respect for the procedural and substantive rights of the accused, due regard being also had for the protection of witnesses and victims. Rule 89(A) makes it clear that a Trial Chamber shall not be bound by national rules of evidence, whether representing the common law or the civil law. As held by the Appeals Chamber in Aleksovski, a judgement delivered on February 16, 1999: "There is no reason to import such rules into the practice of the Tribunal, which is not bound by national rules of evidence ... The purpose of the Rules is to promote a fair and expeditious trial, and the Trial Chambers must have the flexibility to achieve this goal. This Trial Chamber believes that it should not consider itself hindered by technical rules in its search for the truth apart from those listed in Section 3 of the Rules. In the opinion of this Trial Chamber, the most important rule in this context is Rule 89 which lists the general evidentiary provisions, and as already stated, in its Subrule (B) provides that 'in cases not otherwise provided for in the Rules, the Trial Chamber shall apply rules of evidence which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before it and are consonant and in harmony with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law.'" The same rule permits the Chamber to admit any evidence with probative value and exclude any if the probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. This confirms what has already been pointed out, namely that in trial proceedings before this International Tribunal, there seem to be no pre-established technical rules for the admissibility of evidence. It is clear that the approach adopted by the Rules is one which is definitely in favour of the admissibility of evidence provided that this is relevant and has probative value. Needless to say, irrelevant evidence needs to and will be excluded in the most unequivocal way in the interest of a fair and expeditious trial. These considerations have resulted in a generally uniform tendency of the various Trial Chambers of this International Tribunal towards admitting evidence, in the first place, leaving its weight to be assessed when all the evidence is being considered by the Trial Chamber in the final elaboration of its judgement. This approach has also met with the approval of the Appeals Chamber in more than one instance. This will therefore, in principle, be the practice which this Trial Chamber will adopt throughout these proceedings. Another conspicuous practice that has been followed by the Trial Chambers of this International Tribunal and which will be followed by this one is that the common law general rules relating to the exclusion of evidence will not be followed as a rule. The main reason for this is that these rules were conceived in the context of a system of trial by jury where there is the absolute need to keep away from the lay jurors prejudicial material of little or no probative value which it may be difficult for them to erase from their mind. Proceedings before this International Tribunal, as very ably pointed out this morning, are instead conducted by professional judges. This Trial Chamber attaches great importance to this special characteristic of this International Tribunal. The position was also made clear, very clear, by the Trial Chamber in the Delalic decision referred to before, and I quote from paragraph 20: "While the importance of the rules on admissibility in common law follows from the effect which the admission of a certain piece of evidence might have on a group of lay jurors, the trials before the International Tribunal are conducted before professional judges, who by virtue of their training and experience are able to consider each piece of evidence which has been admitted and determine its appropriate weight." Having premised all this, this Trial Chamber will now spell out some of the rules which will govern these proceedings and by which the parties should be guided. The first guideline is that the parties should always bear in mind the basic distinction that exists between the legal admissibility of documentary evidence and the weight that documentary evidence is given in the courtroom. The second guideline is that the fact that this Trial Chamber may at some point in time in the course of these proceedings rule against the admissibility of some particular document or other piece of evidence will not prevent that ruling being reversed contrarily or at a later stage as further evidence emerges. The third guideline is that which was stated in the Delalic decision I referred to earlier, namely that, "The mere admission of a document into evidence does not in itself signify that the statements contained therein will necessarily be deemed to be an accurate portrayal of the facts. Factors such as authenticity or proof of authorship will naturally assume the greatest importance before the Trial Chamber's assessment and during the Trial Chamber's assessment of the weight to be attached to the individual pieces of evidence." Also, this Trial Chamber agrees that "the threshold standard for the admission of evidence should not be set excessively high, as often documents are sought to be admitted into evidence, not as ultimate proof of guilt or innocence, but to provide a context and to complete the picture presented by the evidence in general." This does not mean that either of the parties in pretending the right to have a document admitted in evidence have also the right not to have the reliability of that document questioned at the time of the requested or pretended admission. As stated by the Appeals Chamber in the Delalic decision of the 4th March, 1998, and as this Trial Chamber sees it at the station of admission of evidence, the implicit requirement of reliability means no more than that there must be sufficient indicia of reliability to make out a prima facie case for the admission of that document. This is, however, by far and large substantially different from what counsel for the defence of the two accused are pretending, especially since their submission would in the opinion of this Trial Chamber entail a thorough, if not conclusive, examination not only of indicia of reliability but of practically the absolute authenticity of the document purported to be exhibited. This is not and would not be in accordance with the case law of this International Tribunal. The fourth guideline is that when, as has already happened in this case, objections may be given and taken on grounds of authenticity, this Trial Chamber will follow the practice that has generally been adopted until now by this International Tribunal, namely, generally to admit documents and video recordings and then decide what weight to give them, having seen them, there being no lay jury to protect from prejudicial matter or some other matter which in due course needs to be ruled inadmissible. Always in the same context, the fifth guideline is that the parties should remember that there is no blanket prohibition on the admission of documents simply on the grounds that their purported author has not been called to testify. Similarly, the parties are being reminded that the fact that a document is unsigned or unstamped does not a priori render it void of authenticity. In fact, as rightly pointed out by the learned counsel for the Prosecution this morning, the absence of a signature or of an official seal may sometimes in itself be indicative of the pursuit of a criminal joint enterprise or possibly a way intentionally devised to avoid having the paternity of that document directly established. As already stated, factors such as authenticity and proof of authorship will naturally assume the greatest importance in the Trial Chamber's assessment of the weight to be attached to individual pieces of evidence. This position was further crystallised by the Appeals Chamber in the 4 March, 1998, Delalic decision where it was stated that, "To require absolute proof of a document's authenticity before it could be admitted would be to require a far more stringent test than the standard envisaged by Subrule 8(C)." The sixth guideline refers to an aspect that has already been referred to extensively by the Presiding Judge in this Trial Chamber during his initial address to the parties on the first day of this trial, namely the issue of hearsay evidence. This is an issue which it is anticipated will engage this Trial Chamber from time to time, especially as either of the parties will seek to present statements of persons who have died in the meantime or other similar items of evidence. The position is being reiterated in the words of the Appeals Chamber in the Aleksovski case decision of the 19th of January, 1999, and I quote: "It is well settled in the practice of the Tribunal that hearsay evidence is admissible. Thus, relevant out-of-court statements which a Trial Chamber considers probative are admissible under Rule 89(C). This was established in 1996 by the decision of Trial Chamber II in Prosecutor versus Tadic and followed by Trial Chamber I in Prosecutor versus Blaskic. Neither decision was the subject of appeal and it is not now submitted that they were wrongly decided. Accordingly, Trial Chambers have a broad discretion under Rule 89(C) to admit relevant hearsay evidence. Since such evidence is admitted to prove the truth of its contents, the Trial Chamber must be satisfied that it is reliable for that purpose, in the sense of being voluntary, truthful and trustworthy as appropriate and for this purpose may consider both the content of the hearsay statement and the circumstances under which the evidence arose; or, as Judge Stephen described it, the probative value of a hearsay statement will depend on the context and the character of the evidence in question. The absence of the opportunity to cross-examine the person who made the statements and whether the hearsay is "firsthand" or further removed, are also relevant to the probative value of the evidence, and to these, this Trial Chamber will attach great importance. The fact that the evidence is hearsay does not necessarily deprive it of probative value but it is acknowledged that the weight or probative value to be afforded to that evidence will usually be less than that given to the testimony of a witness who has given it under a form of oath or who has been cross-examined, although even this will depend on the infinitely variable circumstances which surround hearsay evidence." This is the seventh guideline, and later on the aspect of reliability will also be revisited. The eighth guideline is that since it is the responsibility of the Trial Chamber to seek and apply the best rules in its determination of the matter before it, the so-called best evidence rule will be applied. This essentially means that the Trial Chamber will rely on the best evidence available in the circumstances of the case and parties are being directed to regulate the production and the presentation of their evidence along these lines. What is the best evidence will, of course, depend on the particular circumstances attached to each document and to the complexity of this case and the investigations which preceded it. The Trial Chamber will exercise its discretion in the spirit which lies at the basis of the Statute and the Rules. With the ninth guideline, the Trial Chamber draws the attention of the parties to Rule 95 which provides for the exclusion of improperly obtained evidence and declares that no evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission is antithetical to, and would seriously damage, the Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 965 to 966. integrity of these proceedings. Accordingly, the Trial Chamber makes it clear at the very outset that statements which are not voluntary but are obtained from suspects by oppressive conduct cannot pass the test under Rule 95, the burden being on the Prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the statement was voluntary and not obtained by oppressive conduct. As stated in the Delalic case, to which I made reference earlier on, it is extremely difficult for a statement taken in violation of Rule 42 to fall within Rule 95, which protects the integrity of the proceedings by the exclusion of evidence obtained by methods which cast substantial doubts on that integrity. The tenth guideline which this Trial Chamber wishes to draw the attention of the parties to relates to the notion of reliability already mentioned and one that has been emphasised in the course of the oral submissions of this morning. In matters of hearsay evidence, it seems that the Rules implicitly require that reliability be a component of admissibility, and, indeed, following previous case law of this Tribunal on the matter, this Trial Chamber agrees that reliability is an inherent and implicit component of each element of admissibility. This is so because if the evidence offered is unreliable then it cannot be either relevant or of probative value. Therefore, such evidence will be inadmissible in terms of Subrule 89(C). The Trial Chamber, however, wishes to make it clear that it certainly does not agree that the determination of the issue of reliability in this context of hearsay evidence, when it arises, should be seen as a separate, first step in assessing a piece of evidence offered for admission. This has already been decided by the Trial Chamber in the Delalic decision mentioned by me earlier on, and as also illustrated in the Mucic handwriting decision and will be followed by this Trial Chamber. Furthermore, the position was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber, as I explained earlier on, and therefore the notion of establishing indicia of reliability ought not to be confused with having admissibility predicated on the extent of proof of reliability as suggested by counsel for the Defence. That would be tantamount to finding a way round the previous decisions of the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber, which this Trial Chamber is not prepared to do. Last but not least, this Trial Chamber emphasises what it considers to be an overriding principle in matters of admissibility of evidence. The Trial Chamber is, in terms of the Statute, the guardian of the procedural and substantive rights of the accused and has, in addition, the delicate task of striking a balance in seeking to protect also the rights of victims and witnesses. A trial, as we all know, is a delicate and often complex journey in search of the truth, and the Trial Chamber strongly believes that questions of admissibility of evidence do not arise and do not depend solely when one of the parties raises an objection to a piece of evidence sought to be brought forward by the other party. Naturally, when there is no objection, when the authenticity of a document, for example, is not contested, the task of admitting evidence will be made easier, but this Trial Chamber has an inherent right and duty to ensure that only that evidence which under the Rules may be admitted will be admitted, and for this purpose, will, as may turn out to be necessary from time to time, intervene ex officio to exclude from these proceedings those pieces of evidence which, in its opinion, for one or more of the reasons laid down in the Rules, ought not to be admitted in evidence. In other words, this admission of the Prosecution that for a document to be admitted into evidence the Prosecution must establish relevance and probative value is very much in accordance with what the Rules in effect require from either party seeking to introduce a document in evidence. The Prosecution is also right in submitting that it need not establish authenticity or authorship or even the source of a document for such admission, but the Prosecution, as well as the Defence, should always keep in mind that they may be called upon by the Trial Chamber to provide a minimum of proof that would be sufficient to constitute a prima facie indicia of reliability when on the face of it the particular document so warrants, or warrants so. There is a final note that this Trial Chamber would like to make in relation to one of the submissions made by the learned counsel to accused Brdjanin. It is undoubtedly true that this case involves an unusually large number of documents, but the need for specific attention to be given to each document which he suggests and lays emphasis upon, cannot be accepted as a precondition for the admission of these documents. As stated, saving where this Trial Chamber deems it fit to intervene ex officio, the practice will be in favour of admissibility, with other aspects related thereto such as those of relevance and probative value following during the course of the trial. This oral decision, as explained to you earlier on by me, will be incorporated in a properly drawn-up written decision which will be handed down in due course. So now, I think, Ms. Korner, unless there are other matters which you would like to raise at this point, you can proceed with bringing forward your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I do that, in the light of Your Honour's ruling, can I make sure that I understand how the procedure will go. What I propose to do now is to call the lead investigator to explain in general terms the sources of documents. And Your Honour should have got a copy of his statement, plus the various annexes which relate to those documents, which were disclosed to the Defence some time ago. Your Honour, there are a number of documents contained within the binder that Dr. Donia will be referring to which have been objected to, and I was proposing to take the investigator through each of those documents. But it may be, in the light of Your Honour's ruling, that those objections will now be withdrawn. There are a large number of documents, and some of the criteria for the objection, as I say, are slightly obscure. Although some were not signed or whatever, others were, and others are stamped. For future -- not convenience, to make the trial run more smoothly, the suggestion that I was going to make was that if objection is raised to documents that appear in the municipality binders, before we start the evidence on each municipality, the investigator will return, and those objections can be dealt with through the evidence that he can give. However, if no objection is raised to any particular document, then we would suggest that the document is deemed to be agreed to be admitted with all the caveats that Your Honour has gone through. So really what I'm asking at the moment, before I call the investigator, am I required to deal with all the documents that are objected -- that were objected to last Friday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm still kind of working out the Court's ruling and decision. I believe I understand it. I think for purposes of the record that I am still required if I have an objection to a document to lodge that objection, and then the Trial Chamber, as time goes on, can keep revisiting that document to see if they've proved anything more about it that might make it possible for you to decide that it has some relevance or weight or authenticity or anything like that. I think -- I think what Your Honours were saying is that we're just not going to deal with this as a separate matter upfront before we go into the documents. And that's fine. Well, I shouldn't say it's fine. I tend to object to it, because it's different from what I had suggested, and I don't want to give up the position I have on the record that I think it's not possible -- not proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless the document itself on the face of it makes it almost compulsory, obligatory, on this Trial Chamber to seek more information from the Prosecution -- or from the Defence, because what applies to the documents of the Prosecution applies also to the -- all the documents that you will be asking to bring in evidence later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you are exactly in the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think so. And I think I'm in the same position with regard to my objections to the documents. And it appears to me that what must happen at this point is whether or not the Prosecutor puts on any evidence at this point regarding a particular Donia document that I have objected to would depend on whether the Trial Chamber requires additional evidence at this point on that document, it seems to me, rather than as some kind of a rule that that has to happen. So my proposal is that Ms. Korner proceed as she planned to proceed, with the understanding that those documents that I've objected to remain objected to. And if the Court does not see any particular reason to require any additional evidence from her regarding it at this point, then we go forward. And if you do, then she'll have to put it on. I think that's where we are. And maybe I'm wrong, but I think that's where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, more or less we are. I mean, actually, Ms. Korner also preferred to have you go a step further and say, "Okay. There is no need to sustain the -- some of the objections raised earlier, in view of the decision of the Trial Chamber." For example, I mean, one of the objections that you had raised, and also Defence for General Talic, refers to unsigned, unsealed, unstamped documents. I mean, the position which has been explained by the Trial Chamber is at variance with the position that you had taken earlier. And more or less what Ms. Korner wants to know is whether in view of the decision of this Trial Chamber, you are now going to make her life or her task a little bit easier or lighter than it would have been otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can't at this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I read you well, don't I?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour reads me very well indeed. And I was merely trying to move things along a little faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can't at this point change my position, Your Honours, because it's not merely it has no stamp or signature but because it could have been -- those documents tend to have a character to them that you could conclude either that they are real or that somebody typed them in the back room a month ago or six months ago or whenever, because there's nothing on them to indicate that they're anything but a manufactured document. And I think the Court has to look at them and decide with regard to each one, as you suggested this morning, whether you want more evidence from the Prosecutor about it or not. But I wouldn't -- I'm not going to waive objection to documents that I can't tell by looking at them have any kind of authenticity at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We also maintain our objections for the same reasons presented by my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Ms. Korner, now you know exactly what is expected from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. In that event, some time ago the Defence were given a copy of the index and indeed -- I'm sorry, a copy of the index to the Banja Luka selection of documents. They will be given today the list that the first fact witness is going to refer to. Before we start the Banja Luka evidence, I would ask again that we be supplied with a list of the documents which are objected to, and we will go through the same procedure as today. May I say that Mr. Ackerman has already provided me - I'm not sure if it's complete - but certainly with a list of those documents, which he's doing the other way round, for which, as he puts it, he waives foundation. Your Honour, in that event, I now call Mazhar Inayat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Inayat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. You will now be handed a sheet of paper containing a statement you are required to make before you start your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine you are familiar to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the first time I am testifying, but yes, I do know the procedures here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you need any clarification, the Chamber will give it to you. We are the Judges composing this Chamber. You have been summoned here as a witness for the Prosecution. The Prosecution is to your right. And Ms. Joanna Korner will be conducting her examination-in-chief of yourself. And on your left are two Defence teams, for each of the accused respectively. To the extreme left, your left, is Defence team for General Talic, and to the right, it's the Defence team for Mr. Brdjanin. Mr. Brdjanin is at the back on the -- your left, and General Talic is on your right at the back. So you can proceed with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, is your name Mazhar Inayat?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For the purposes of the record, your surname is spelled I-N-A-Y-A-T?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For how long have you been working as an investigator with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor employed me as an investigator on 9th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Subsequently, were you promoted to the position of team leader in charge of a number of investigators?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: That is correct. In December of 1997, I was promoted as investigations team leader, and since then, I have held this position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, are you now working with what is called Team 1?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Team 1 is the one that I'm heading, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And could you just tell Their Honours what is Team 1's area of investigation?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: From the very beginning, Team 1 has been investigating war crimes that were committed in the northwestern region of Bosnia, which is also sometimes referred to as Bosanska Krajina, and in 1992, this region also became to be known as the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think it's right that you have dealt, or the team and you also, have dealt with the investigations and subsequent prosecutions in the case of Tadic, Kvocka and Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: That is correct. But I just need to clarify that although my team did investigate the case against Sikirica, but it was then -- before it was prosecuted in the Court, it was transferred to another team.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the purpose of your testimony today, Mr. Inayat, is to deal with the question of the document seizures in this case. Were you asked, in December of last year, to go through the exhibit list which had been handed to the Court and the Defence, and asked to ascertain the source of each of the documents listed?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: That is correct, that I spent almost several weeks reviewing the documents which had been listed in the exhibit list, which I believe are over 3300 documents, and I did try to locate the sources of each and every document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you supply, with your statement, the exhibit list annotated with the source, as you were able to establish it, of each of the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And also a guide to the annotations you used to show where each document came from?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Yes. I did create a legend and I did describe that legend in Annex B in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we deal, please, with the source of the major document collections? I think it's right that the team conducted search and seizure operations in the field.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: There were three search and seizure operations conducted by the team.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there two in the town of Prijedor and one in the town of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you deal first of all, please, with the seizure that took place first of all in the town of Prijedor? When did that happen, the first one?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: The first Prijedor search and seizure took place on 12th of December, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And at which locations was the operation conducted?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: The team searched four locations in Prijedor town. Those locations were the municipal building, the police station, the SDS offices, and finally the radio station building which also housed the premises for Kozarski Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, on the board, you will see there is a plan of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it may assist Your Honours - I hope you can see it - if Mr. Inayat were to point out the various locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you point out, is the map visible on your -- can you see it from there? And is it visible on your monitors? Mr. Ackerman, can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have a blow-up of the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that was as large as we could get it. We could -- what we could probably do -- [B/C/S interpretation] -- not in court. Oh, they are in court. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That makes it easier, because otherwise it will be difficult from any distance to follow what you will be showing on that map in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think probably it's easier -- we can distribute copies if necessary, but it's easier at the moment if we perhaps put it on the ELMO and then we will distribute copies thereafter. If we put that on the ELMO and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can work that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, this is the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, I think you have to indicate it actually on the ELMO itself and point to it, and that should come up.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I'm afraid the details --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you can point first of all to the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, I don't know how to point this out. I mean, can I do it on the map perhaps, on the big one? And I can give the numbers, in fact, on the big map, which perhaps would be easier for you to follow on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will be difficult also for us to follow, because that map is at quite a distance. Can't you use the document on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, this is a town map of Prijedor town, and Prijedor -- on the top of the page, you can see Prijedor which is the northern direction. Bosanska Dubica is in that direction. On the east of Prijedor town is Banja Luka, and there is a road coming from Banja Luka into Prijedor, Banja Luka being about 48 kilometres from Prijedor. This main road goes right through the centre of the heart of Prijedor, and Prijedor town is in the centre, in the built-up area. This is where most of the government buildings are located. I don't know if you can see number 11. That's the municipal building. The number 11 is in red.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Ms. Korner, I think it is high time we have those maps distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Since the witness is going to refer to specific points from that map, I think we ought to have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he simply draws a circle around it with a pencil, we can probably then see it on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if this pointer is showing on -- yes, it is. This is the Banja Luka road which is coming into Prijedor and we have just passed Keraterm camp which is to the right of this road. And this road goes right through the heart of Prijedor town and then south towards Sanski Most. Now, this area that we are looking at is where all the government buildings are located and this is also the centre of Prijedor. Building number 11, which is this, Your Honours, is the municipal building which is three storeyed, and the police station is right opposite this road. In fact, this road, which is the main Banja Luka-Prijedor road at this point is also called Jovan Raskovic Road. It is at this location that the municipal building and the Prijedor Police Station are located. Then we have the radio station which is, Your Honours, this building here, and probably if you can see this number 23 written beside this building. This is where the Kozarski Vjesnik offices were also located and the radio station. Your Honours, this road here, which I am pointing out with my pointer, is the Vozd Karadjordje Road and the street address, Vozd Karadjordje 16, is the place where the SDS offices were located, and in fact there are too many small dots here. One of these buildings, I would say. Here, Your Honours, is where the SDS offices were located. So, Your Honours, these were the four locations where we went on 12th of December, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Inayat. Your Honour, I think that probably ought to be marked as an exhibit now, that document. Perhaps that could be made Prosecutor's Exhibit number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be entered as P1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Inayat, the search and seizure operation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please. Microphone, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The search and seizure operation that was carried out, was that pursuant to a search warrant that had been issued by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Yes. On 8th of December, Judge Fouad Riad issued the search warrants, and pursuant to those search warrants, these four locations were searched.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I think we can deal with the operation itself fairly quickly. There was a team consisting of investigators, lawyers, analysts and language staff?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: That is correct. We, in fact, had four teams simultaneously going into these four locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you personally were involved in the search of the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I personally was involved in the search of the municipal building. But once it was concluded in the evening, I also went and searched premises in the police station then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think the operation itself lasted one full day.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: That's correct. We also started at about 9.30, 10.00, searching these locations. And by 7.00, 7.30, we had collected the evidence we wanted to receive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the documents, which in total I think you estimated numbered about 40.000, were those sealed in boxes?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: I'd just like to correct myself, because I think I did say this to you once, that there were 40.000 documents. But actually, I'd like to clarify that. It was 53.000 pages of documents that were seized from those four locations, of course the major chunk coming from the police station. And yes, they were sealed into cardboard boxes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before we deal with the other searches and seizures, can you just explain the system of how these documents were seized and placed into boxes?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT
utterances.text: Yes. What we did before the searches commenced was that each search party had an investigator assigned as the custodian officer, and that person was supposed to sit in a central location and receive documents which had been brought by other investigators and lawyers. For example, I was the custodian for the municipal building search and seizure, and we searched three rooms of the office of the mayor, which is on the first floor, room number 21; the office of the president of the executive board, room number 29; and their secretary's office; and another archive's room. As the documents were being brought to me, I was filling out evidence register forms of procedure that we have to adopt when we are seizing material. In the evidence register form, I was identifying the material -- mainly -- I have to point out that when we had started this search and seizure, we had expected that hopefully we will be able to describe in detail each and every piece of document that we are going to lift. But by midday, we had realised that the sheer amount of documents that we were going to seize will not make that possible. So as the folders and the books and the documents were being brought to me, I would register them on the evidence register form, and I would take custody. And the cardboard boxes which were lying right next to me, I placed those -- that material in the cardboard boxes. Once this had been done by about 4.00, 5.00 in the evening in the municipal building, we took those boxes with us to the base where we were staying. And this is a procedure that was also followed at the other three locations.
